thesis: I bought Lantheus because it's the toll booth every prostate patient passes through before treatment, still growing volume at ~18.6x free cash flow. I think the market is overreacting to temporary manufacturing worries and underrating management's execution. I'm accepting that CMS and insurers set the price, not the company. I'd rethink this if the pass-through clock expires soon or price per scan slips.
risks: Pricing is controlled by CMS and insurers, not Lantheus; pass-through status can reset margin overnight.

lifecycle.open_note: High-quality radiopharma leader with a proven execution track record trading below my estimate of intrinsic value. I belive the market is overreacting to temporary manufacturing concerns while underestimating management's long-term growth targets.

drafts.x_post: $LNTH is a regulated cash machine, not a growth-pharma stock — its moat protects scan volume but not price, and price is the whole valuation. The kill-switch is a calendar fact, not vague dread. Dead Simple Score: 81/100. Watchlist until the reimbursement clock is confirmed.
video_talking_points: Lantheus makes the tracers doctors inject so prostate cancer lights up on a scan before treatment.
The stock has run hard and now trades at a price that already assumes a slowdown, with the next earnings call as the first real check on pricing.
It's a toll booth every prostate patient passes through, growing volume as PSMA-PET becomes standard of care, and throwing off cash on a clean balance sheet.
The catch: Lantheus doesn't control its own pricing — when pass-through status expires, per-dose margin can collapse even as scan volume rises.
The load-bearing fact, the reimbursement clock, is unverified — so committing capital now is buying blind.
Verdict: watch, and flip it to a small check once the pass-through date and Aug 4 pricing confirm.
